record.paper_title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data: Challenges, Initial Promise, and Open Questions
record.original_question: For networking datasets in which each sample contains fixed metadata together with an associated multivariate time series, can generative adversarial networks be used to create synthetic datasets that remain high-fidelity and generalize across downstream networking tasks without requiring substantial human expertise about workload characteristics or target tasks?

evidence.quote: The overarching question for our work is: Can we create high-fidelity, easily generalizable synthetic datasets for networking applications that require minimal (if any) human expertise regarding workload characteristics and downstream tasks?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider datasets of the form $\mathcal{D}=\{(m_i, x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, where each sample consists of fixed-dimensional metadata $m_i \in \mathcal{M}$ (categorical and/or continuous attributes) and an associated multivariate time series $x_i = (x_i^{(1)}, \dots, x_i^{(T_i)})$ with $x_i^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and possibly variable length $T_i$. Such datasets arise in networking contexts (e.g., traffic measurements, system telemetry, user session traces) and exhibit features such as heterogeneous metadata distributions, long-range temporal correlations, multi-scale behavior, and strong coupling between metadata and time-series dynamics.

A generative model $G_\theta$ is said to produce a synthetic dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ that is "high-fidelity and task-generalizable" if, for a broad family $\mathcal{T}$ of downstream predictive or analytic tasks (each specified by a loss $\ell_T$ and an algorithm $A_T$ trained on a dataset), the performance gap
$$\Delta(T) = \big| \mathbb{E}[\ell_T(A_T(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}))] - \mathbb{E}[\ell_T(A_T(\mathcal{D}))] \big|$$
is uniformly small over $T \in \mathcal{T}$, and if standard distributional fidelity metrics (marginal distributions of metadata, autocorrelation functions of time series, joint metadata–time-series statistics) on $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ closely match those of $\mathcal{D}$.

Question: Does there exist a generative-adversarial-network–based procedure $G_\theta$, trained on $\mathcal{D}$ without task-specific supervision and without dataset-specific feature engineering or hand-crafted workload assumptions, such that for arbitrary networking datasets of the above form the resulting synthetic dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ is high-fidelity and task-generalizable in the sense above? Equivalently, characterize the conditions on $\mathcal{D}$, on the GAN architecture, and on the training procedure under which such universal high-fidelity, task-agnostic synthetic data generation is achievable.
artifact.category_tag: Generative adversarial networks for time-series synthesis
artifact.status_search_result: The question of building GAN-based synthetic data generators for networked time series that are high-fidelity and generalize across downstream tasks without manual feature engineering remains an active and open research area. Follow-up work (e.g., DoppelGANger and subsequent improvements) reports progress on specific datasets but acknowledges persistent challenges in privacy, mode coverage, long time-series fidelity, and cross-task generalization, indicating the broader question is not resolved.

status_evidence.title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data (DoppelGANger)
status_evidence.snippet: Presents DoppelGANger as initial promise toward synthetic networked time series and explicitly lists open questions on fidelity, generalization, and privacy.
status_evidence.claim: The framing as 'initial promise and open questions' indicates the overarching problem is posed as open.

status_evidence.title: Practical GAN-based Synthetic IP Header Trace Generation using NetShare
status_evidence.snippet: Subsequent work building on DoppelGANger reports continued improvements but also remaining limitations in cross-task fidelity for networking traces.
status_evidence.claim: Active follow-up indicates the broad question remains unresolved.
